title: The stolen blessing (Genesis 27)
hookLine: goat skins, a blind father, and Esau's cry "Bless me, even me also, O my father"

lines: A BLIND FATHER, A FAVORITE SON.
cards: Isaac is old, and his eyes have gone dim. He calls in Esau, his favorite: go hunt, make me the tasty food I love, so I can bless you before I die. Rebekah is listening.
She calls Jacob, her favorite, with a plan. Bring me two young goats; I'll cook them the way your father likes, and he'll bless you instead. Jacob hesitates.
Esau is hairy and I'm smooth. If he touches me, I'll be caught, and I'll get a curse, not a blessing. His mother answers, in the old JPS translation: "Upon me be thy curse, my son."
She dresses him in Esau's best clothes, and covers his hands and neck with goat skins.

teach.h: THE VOICE OF JACOB, HANDS OF ESAU.
teach.b: Jacob goes in. Who are you, my son? I'm Esau, your firstborn.
Isaac is uneasy. How did you find game so fast? Come close, let me feel you.
He touches the goat-skin hands and says one of the most well-known lines in Genesis: "The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau."
He blesses him anyway: the dew of heaven, the richness of the earth, may nations serve you. Jacob has barely left when Esau walks in with the meal. Who are you?
I am your son, your firstborn, Esau.
And the Torah says Isaac "trembled very exceedingly." Esau understands, and cries out with a great and bitter cry: "Bless me, even me also, O my father."
And again: "Hast thou but one blessing, my father?" And he lifts up his voice and weeps. It's one of the most painful moments in the Torah, and the rabbis didn't look away.
A midrash says Esau's cry was answered centuries later, in the book of Esther, when Mordecai, a descendant of Jacob, cries out in Persia with a great and bitter cry, the same words.
The passed-over brother's tears were not forgotten.
Readers argue about Rebekah: some say she acted on the prophecy that the elder would serve the younger; others see a family broken by favorites. Everyone here deceives or is deceived.
But the voice that stays is Esau's, asking for what every child asks for: a blessing of my own.

how: Jews read this story in the Torah portion Toldot; on Friday nights many Jewish parents place their hands on their children's heads and bless each of them, one by one.

s: Isaac was completely fooled, with no suspicion
he was uneasy: the voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau.
when Esau came in, Isaac trembled very exceedingly
the Torah says so, and then Esau cries out, bless me, even me also.

games.q: you're Jacob. your mother has a plan to get your father's blessing, but you're afraid of being caught and cursed. what does she say?
o: "upon me be thy curse, my son."
games.why: she takes the risk on herself, dresses him in Esau's clothes and goat skins, and sends him in.

practice: Picture someone in your life who feels passed over: the sibling who wasn't the favorite, the coworker who missed the promotion, the kid picked last, the parent nobody calls.
Hear their question, is there a blessing for me too, and hold them for a minute with care, even though you can't undo what happened. If you pray, you can bless them in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Esau, the brother who came home too late and cried out, bless me, even me also, O my father.

orig.note: Hebrew: bless me, me too, my father. Esau's cry (27:34).

carryVoice: Your line: bless me too. A line for anyone who's ever been passed over. See you tomorrow.
